          GOOGLE LLC’S RESPONSE AND OBJECTION TO OG&E’S MOTION
            TO STRIKE PORTIONS OF THE RESPONSIVE TESTIMONY OF
                           ADRIAN J. KIMBROUGH

                Google LLC objects to Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company’s (“OG&E”) motion to strike

         portions of Adrian J. Kimbrough’s responsive testimony and respectfully requests that the

         Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) deny the requested wholesale exclusion. In the alternative,

         Google asks the ALJ to preserve testimony concerning the operation, economics, and tariff design

         of the proposed self-supply framework while reserving disputed legal conclusions to later in the

         procedural schedule. Ultimately, the ALJ and Commissioners should only adopt technical and

         legal conclusions after considering both testimony presented by experts and argument presented

         by counsel.


                         I.      The motion and the proper scope of the objection.

                1.      OG&E asks the ALJ to strike portions of Kimbrough’s responsive testimony at

         pages 52:6–53:22 or, alternatively, to disregard the cited questions and answers when determining

         legal issues. OG&E argues that Kimbrough, who acknowledges he is not an attorney, opines on

         the legality of self-supply; the Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act; retail choice and
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 55 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 7




         wheeling; HB2992; Commission authority; and the claimed precedential effect or approval of

         proceedings involving a proposed joint stipulation. OG&E expressly does not challenge his

         qualifications in utility economics, tariff design, cost allocation, and related subjects. OG&E’s

         Mot. to Strike ¶¶ 2–7, 10–13 (filed Sept. 22, 2026, Entry No. 43).

                2.       The motion identifies a distinction between technical evidence and legal advocacy,

         but a witness’s lack of a law degree is not itself a rule of exclusion. The Commission’s hearing

         rule permits authenticated prepared testimony subject to cross-examination. It ordinarily applies

         Oklahoma district-court evidence rules, permits relaxation in the public interest, and authorizes

         exclusion of evidence or its receipt subject to final Commission ruling. The rule does not require

         a PUD witness to be an attorney. Okla. Admin. Code § 165:5-13-3(f), (h), (k), (p). That does not

         mean a nonlawyer’s legal interpretation controls. The ALJ may separate a witness’s technical

         description from a disputed legal proposition and leave the latter to counsel and the Commission.


         II.     OG&E’s own large-load testimony demonstrates why a categorical objection
                                           is misplaced.

                3.       Gwin Cash, OG&E’s Senior Manager of Pricing, Rate Administration, and Load

         Analysis holds a bachelor’s degree in applied mathematics, not a law degree. Cash Direct Test.

         2:9–26 (Entry No. 3). In supporting OG&E’s XLPL tariff and terms, Cash states that they are

         “consistent with the requirements” of HB2992 and “in compliance with” Final Order No. 753440.

         Id. 3:3–12. Those are affirmative conclusions applying statutory and Commission-order

         requirements to the very large-load filing under review. OG&E cannot persuasively maintain that

         the same sort of legal-compliance characterization, when advanced by a nonlawyer supporting

         Google’s alternative proposal, requires exclusion of that witness’s related technical evidence.

                4.       Matthew DeCourcey, OG&E’s large-load consultant holds degrees in political

         science and business administration, not law. DeCourcey Direct Test. 2:13–3:3 (Entry No. 4). He

         testifies that the proposed tariff envisions no bounds on the scope of the Commission’s review and

         no expectation of limits on steps the Commission might take in response to adverse impacts on

         other customer classes. Id. 22:1–12.

                5.       OG&E’s direct testimony itself asks the Commission to consider their non-legal

         expert’s legal conclusions violating what OGE argues is the limitations on expert testimony.

         OG&E’s argument against such testimony is wrong. To the extent expert testimony includes legal

         conclusions, the ALJ and Commissioners may consider that testimony in light of a party’s overall

         arguments contained in their filings and give that testimony the weight it deserves.


             III.    Comparable testimony in other PUD proceeding related to Large Load
                         Tariffs reinforces the need for a consistent standard.

                6.       In Case No. PUD2025-000075, Attorney General witness Brice D. Betchan held

         accounting degrees and a CPA credential, not a law degree. Betchan Responsive Test. 7:7–13

         (Entry No. 138). He interprets IRS Revenue Procedure 2020-39 as allowing the Commission to

         use any reasonable method to determine the net-operating-loss carryforward deferred-tax asset

         attributable to accelerated depreciation and describes a later IRS private letter ruling as confirming

         the Commission’s discretion. Id. 23:3–20. He further characterizes the six-month post-test-year

         limit for certain known and measurable changes as “required by statute.” Id. 26:15–23. Those

         statements do not merely calculate an accounting adjustment: they describe the asserted effect of

         legal authority on the Commission’s available methods and the statutory basis for a ratemaking

         recommendation.

                 7.       Attorney General witness Todd F. Bohrmann holds economics and business-

         administration degrees, not a law degree. Bohrmann Responsive Test. 7:7–10 (Entry No. 141). He

         describes the Commission’s historical exclusion of long-term incentive-plan costs from utility

         revenue requirements and the reasons for that practice. Id. 45:1–9.

                 8.       These are filed testimony comparisons and not proof that the Commission adopted

         any witness’s interpretation, ruled on an objection, or accorded the testimony precedential effect.

         These comparisons instead expose the overbreadth of a proposed nonlawyer qualification rule that

         would threaten ordinary regulatory testimony whenever it discusses a statute, an order, or the

         Commission’s potential response to a tariff proposal.


           IV.        Any discrete legal conclusions can be addressed without striking technical
                                                   evidence.

                 9.       OG&E’s objection should be tested against what a particular sentence is offered to

         prove. It should not be treated as a disqualification of Kimbrough as a witness. His testimony about

         the proposed self-supply framework’s operation, service arrangements, charges, and tariff design

         remains within the subjects OG&E concedes he is qualified to address. References to the

         regulatory setting may assist the Commission in evaluating that proposal without determining

         whether Oklahoma law ultimately authorizes it. Cross-examination and targeted objections allow

         the ALJ to keep the evidentiary and legal questions separate. Okla. Admin. Code § 165:5-13-3(f),

         (h), (k).

                 10.      Google does not ask the Commission to treat a witness’s assertion that self-supply

         is lawful—or an assertion that another proceeding supplies “direct and binding” precedent—as

         dispositive proof of Oklahoma law. The reported status and legal effect of any proposed joint

         stipulation should be resolved from the actual orders and legal briefing, not witness

         characterization. This response does not assert that a final order approved the joint stipulation. If

         the ALJ determines that an identified statement is a pure legal conclusion, the proportionate course

         is to give it no independent weight on the legal issue or receive it subject to final ruling, while

         retaining separable technical testimony. The rule expressly allows receipt of contested evidence

         subject to final Commission ruling and permits legal briefing. Okla. Admin. Code § 165:5-13-3(f),

         (p).


                                             V.      Requested relief

                11.      Google respectfully requests that the ALJ deny OG&E’s motion insofar as it seeks

         to strike or disregard wholesale Kimbrough’s testimony at pages 52:6–53:22. Alternatively, the

         ALJ should identify any discrete legal proposition and give that proposition the weight it deserves

         only after the parties fully present their arguments pursuant to the procedural schedule.
